content: In December 2012, the FDA approved VariZIG, a varicella zoster immune globulin preparation, for use in the United States. This product is intended for post-exposure prophylaxis of varicella in individuals at high risk for severe disease who lack evidence of immunity to varicella and for whom the varicella vaccine is contraindicated. Previously available under an investigational new drug protocol, VariZIG is a purified immune globulin derived from human plasma containing high levels of anti-varicella-zoster virus antibodies (immunoglobulin G). It is currently the only varicella zoster immune globulin preparation available in the United States. VariZIG is recommended to be administered as soon as possible following exposure to the varicella-zoster virus, ideally within 96 hours (4 days) for maximum effectiveness. The CDC advises administration within 10 days of exposure. The CDC has also updated its recommendations to align with those of the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP), extending the eligibility period for premature infants from exposures during the neonatal period to exposures occurring throughout their hospitalization for prematurity. Studies from the late 1960s demonstrated that clinical varicella could be prevented in susceptible, healthy children by administering zoster immune globulin (ZIG) within 72 hours of household exposure. ZIG also reduced attack rates and disease severity in susceptible immunocompromised children when administered within 72 hours of exposure. The first commercial varicella zoster immune globulin preparation, VZIG, became available in the United States in 1978. It was shown to be equivalent to ZIG in preventing or modifying clinical illness in susceptible immunocompromised children if administered within 96 hours of exposure. However, the effectiveness of VZIG when administered beyond 96 hours was not evaluated. In 2006, the supply of VZIG was discontinued, and a new product, VariZIG, became available under an investigational protocol for administration within 96 hours of exposure. In 2011, the FDA approved an amendment to extend the administration period for VariZIG to 10 days after exposure. Subsequent CDC guidance supported administration as soon as possible and within 10 days of exposure. Evidence of immunity to varicella includes documentation of age-appropriate vaccination, laboratory evidence of immunity or confirmation of disease, birth in the United States before 1980 (with exceptions for certain groups), or a healthcare provider's diagnosis or verification of a history of varicella or herpes zoster. For immunocompromised children aged 12 months to 6 years, two doses of varicella vaccine are considered age-appropriate. Limited data from studies outside the United States suggest that administration of immune globulins with high anti-varicella-zoster virus antibody levels beyond 4 days (up to 10 days) after exposure results in comparable varicella incidence and disease attenuation. Based on these findings, the CDC recommends administering VariZIG as soon as possible and within 10 days of exposure. The AAP also supports this recommendation. VariZIG is recommended for high-risk individuals without evidence of immunity to varicella who have been exposed to varicella or herpes zoster and for whom the varicella vaccine is contraindicated. This includes immunocompromised patients, hospitalized premature infants born at ≥28 weeks of gestation whose mothers lack evidence of immunity, hospitalized premature infants born at <28 weeks of gestation or weighing ≤1,000 g at birth regardless of maternal immunity, and pregnant women without evidence of immunity. VariZIG is supplied in 125-IU vials and should be administered intramuscularly as directed by the manufacturer. The recommended dose is 125 IU per 10 kg of body weight, up to a maximum of 625 IU (five vials). Patients eligible for vaccination should receive the varicella vaccine at least 5 months after VariZIG administration. Because VariZIG may prolong the incubation period by at least one week, recipients should be closely monitored for signs and symptoms of varicella for 28 days after exposure. Antiviral therapy should be initiated immediately if varicella symptoms occur. The most common adverse reactions to VariZIG are pain at the injection site and headache, each occurring in approximately 2% of cases. Contraindications include a history of anaphylactic or severe systemic reactions to human immune globulins and IgA-deficient patients with antibodies against IgA and a history of hypersensitivity. The demand for VariZIG has declined significantly due to the decreasing incidence of varicella. However, exposures to varicella and herpes zoster may still occur. Extending the administration window for VariZIG increases the availability of post-exposure prophylaxis for high-risk individuals. Physicians are reminded to administer VariZIG as soon as possible following exposure. The CDC's recommendations for VariZIG use are now harmonized with those of the AAP.
